1:
The address is to two men, and every witness stops on the second name. reformed John Gill notes that the one was the chief magistrate and the other the high priest, and both were concerned to see these laws executed; wesleyan-arminian John Wesley divides the labour between them — the priest was to direct the people where a doubt arose, and the magistrate to see the direction followed. grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott finds a delicacy in the timing: Aaron had just been publicly rebuked, and lest that diminish his standing with the people he was about to teach, the LORD here honours him by making the communication to both conjointly. puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry says the same more simply — now that Aaron was consecrated, God appointed the two as joint commissioners, since it was particularly required of the priests that they should put a difference between clean and unclean.

Keil and Delitzsch set the chapter in its place in the book. The sacrifices and the priesthood had opened the way of access to God's grace; what follows is a body of instruction about the things that hinder that fellowship — sin having its seat in the soul but pervading the body as the soul's organ, and its effects having spread from man to the whole earthly creation, which God subjected to vanity on man's account (Romans 8:20-21). wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke connects it backwards instead, to the prohibition of wine laid on the priests in the previous chapter and the reason given for it — that they might be able at all times to distinguish between clean and unclean, and be fit to teach the people (Leviticus 10:10-11).

Why such a law should exist at all is the question Henry puts bluntly, and answers at length. That God would have it so is reason enough, his will being his wisdom; he saw good to try the obedience of his people not only at the altar but at their own table, as he had tried Adam in innocency by forbidding one tree. Beyond that Henry offers two more: that most of the forbidden meats were really unwholesome, so that God dealt with Israel as a loving father does with children he restrains from what will make them sick; and that a diet peculiar to themselves would keep them from familiar conversation with idolatrous neighbours, the Egyptians having already refused to eat with the Hebrews (Genesis 43:32). Gill and Wesley both include health, Wesley adding that the Jews were especially subject to leprosies. Henry adds a further observation from the learned: that many of the creatures here made unclean were precisely those the heathen held in veneration — the swine sacred to Venus, the owl to Minerva, the eagle to Jupiter — so that Israel might keep up a religious loathing of what the Gentiles superstitiously valued.

Calvin will have none of the medical reading, and says so in the sharpest sentence in the chapter: those who imagine that God here had regard to their health, as if he were discharging the office of a physician, pervert by their vain speculation the whole force and use of this law. He allows that the permitted meats are wholesome and best adapted for food. But the preface, in which God tells the people he has chosen them for holiness, and the later abolition of the law together show that this was part of the elementary instruction under which God kept his ancient people — a shadow of things to come, whose body is Christ (Colossians 2:16-17). Clarke, quoting Bishop Wilson, draws a different evidence from the same separation: no art of man could have held so turbulent a nation to precepts so troublesome, had they not been convinced from the first that the command was God's.
3:
Two marks are named, and they must meet. Gill is precise about the first: the hoof must be parted and cloven quite through, since there are creatures whose feet are divided above but joined underneath by a skin — which is why both phrases are used. Ellicott renders it more exactly still — whatsoever is clovenfooted and entirely separateth the hoofs — and gives the test its examples: the ox, the sheep and the goat are divided below as much as above, while the foot of the dog or the cat or the lion, for all its distinct toes, is united below by a membrane and so fails. The parallel law puts it as cleaving the cleft into two claws (Deuteronomy 14:6).

On the second mark Clarke turns naturalist, and the digression is the fullest thing in the chapter. He walks the food through the four stomachs of the ox — the paunch, where grass is collected unmasticated and macerated by the muscular coats; the honeycomb, with its five-sided cells; the many-plies, with its thin membranous partitions; and the fourth, where digestion is completed and the chyle formed. Chewing the cud is the return of the ball of food up the gullet to be made small a second time, and the purpose of it is that the food should be so comminuted as to yield the greatest possible portion of nutritive juice. Keil and Delitzsch supply the Hebrew: the word for rumination comes from a root meaning to draw to and fro, hence to bring the food up again, and the two clauses are joined so as to mark that both conditions must hold together. Wesley says the same in a line, that both properties are necessary, and that the reason must be resolved into the will of the lawgiver.

What the two marks might signify is where the witnesses become careful. Calvin reports the old reading — the cloven hoof for prudence in distinguishing the mysteries of scripture, the chewing of the cud for serious meditation on its doctrine — and says he neither finds fault with it nor refuses it, while flatly rejecting the subtlety the ancients added, that to divide the word rightly means eliciting mystical senses from the letter, which has licensed every kind of imagination. His own version is plainer: those who have a taste only for the carnal sense do not divide the hoof, since only the spiritual man discerns all things (1 Corinthians 2:15), and the chewing must follow if the food is to be digested — for many gulp down scripture without profit, satisfied with the empty delights of knowledge and making no effort to conform their life to it. Henry offers the same pairing in his own terms, meditation for the cud and justice and charity for the divided hoof, and insists that neither will do without the other: good affections in the heart and good works in the life, or we are not clean.

Calvin then undercuts his own allegory with a candour worth keeping. Why God should have appointed these two things as signs, he says, is no more clear to him than why he forbade the eating of swine — unless perhaps because the solid hoof is a mark of wildness, and the animals that do not ruminate feed for the most part on filth. Wesley reaches the same reserve by a shorter road, calling the interpretations guesses.
4:
Four animals are named to illustrate the rule by failing it, and the grammar of the failure matters. Ellicott corrects the English in each case — though he cheweth the cud, yet he divideth not. Gill states the principle: these are the creatures to which one of the two descriptive characters belongs but not the other. Calvin draws from that the point of the whole arrangement — that partial and imperfect purity must not be obtruded upon God, who demands a cleanness undefiled by any admixture.

The first three fail the same test. Ellicott describes the camel, cloven-footed above but with its toes united below in a large elastic pad like the sole of a shoe, and notes that the Egyptians refused its flesh as heating while the Persians and Arabians feasted on it; Wesley calls it a usual food in Arabia yielding bad nourishment. Keil and Delitzsch account for the same foot by the ball behind, on which the camel treads.

What the coney is, nobody can quite agree. Clarke denies it is the rabbit at all, taking the Hebrew for a creature abounding in Judea and Arabia that Shaw called the daman Israel and Bruce the ashkoko, and passing on Bochart's conjecture that the Phoenicians named Spain from the multitude of these animals found there. Ellicott keeps the rabbit, on the ground that the men who had to administer this law at the time of Christ lived in Palestine and saw the animals, and that they noticed the habit of the feeble conies of sheltering in the fissures of the rocks; he reports that modern expositors identify it instead with the Syrian hyrax or rock-badger. Clarke suspects several species are gathered under both this word and the word for hare.

Whether these creatures ruminate at all is the sharper question, and two witnesses meet it head on. Keil and Delitzsch grant that modern naturalists deny it, since the hare and the hyrax lack the four stomachs of true ruminants; but they move the jaw in a way that looks like rumination, so that even Linnaeus affirmed the hare chewed the cud — and Moses, they conclude, followed the popular opinion. Ellicott says the same and gives the reason: the lawgiver's object was to furnish the people with marks by which they could tell clean from unclean, so he necessarily adopted those in common vogue, which alone were intelligible then.

The swine fails from the other side, and draws more comment than the rest together. Gill notes its hoof is cloven quite through, so it answers the first mark exactly. Ellicott observes that the abhorrence of it infinitely surpasses the repulsion felt for any other unclean beast: eating pork counted as renouncing the law, which is why Antiochus adopted it as the test of apostasy, and why Eleazar spat it forth and chose to die rather than live stained with such an abomination. During the commonwealth there were no swine in Judea, and it was in a far country that the prodigal was sent to feed them. Calvin adds why the prohibition bit hardest here — pork is pleasant and feeds the working classes cheaply — and passes on the mot of Augustus, that he would rather be Herod's pig than his son. Clarke lists its gluttony and filthiness and its sacredness to Venus among the Romans.

The last clause forbids the touch as well as the meal, and two witnesses guard it from overstatement. Keil and Delitzsch limit the carcase to an animal that had died, and note that the same rule applied to clean animals dying of themselves. Wesley denies it is absolute: it forbids touching with a view to eating, and since the fat and skins of some forbidden creatures were useful and were used by good men, God cannot have meant them thrown away.
9:
The water creatures get the shortest rule in the chapter and the fewest examples. Ellicott notes what is missing: for the land animals two criteria were given and fourteen species named, but here not a single fish is identified, and the law is put in the briefest and most generic form possible — leaving those who administered it to define it for practical life. What they produced he sets out in four rules from the second Temple: scales imply fins, so a fish showing scales may be eaten while fins without scales will not do; clean fishes have a complete vertebral column where the unclean have single joints joined by a gelatinous cord; the head of the clean is broad and of the unclean pointed; and the swimming bladder of a clean fish is rounded at one end and pointed at the other. He adds that the parable of the net, drawn from Jewish life, turns on exactly this sorting — the fishermen sat down to separate the good from the bad (Matthew 13:48).

Keil and Delitzsch draw the consequences plainly. Everything in the water that is not a fish — crabs, salamanders and the like — falls outside, and so do fishes without scales, eels for example; they note that Numa forbade the Romans to offer scaleless fish, and that in Egypt they are still thought unwholesome. Ellicott extends the exclusion to shellfish and cetaceans. Clarke gives the reason he thinks lies behind it, that fish covered with a thick glutinous matter instead of scales are very difficult of digestion.

Calvin meets that reading again, and again refuses it. Some who know little of religion plausibly contend that God is acting the physician's part and distinguishing wholesome food from unwholesome; their opinion, he says, is sufficiently refuted by medical men themselves, and even were it granted they would be reasoning badly, since God's purpose was other than to provide for the people's health. Having to deal with a rude people, he chose common marks by which they might gradually ascend to higher things.

Why no fish is named draws three different answers. Calvin's is geographical: most of them were simply unknown to the Jews, whose country produced few river fish, having scarcely any river but the Jordan, while the sea fish only visited the neighbouring shores. Wesley gives that reason and adds another — that most of them wanted names at all, the fish not having been brought to Adam to be named as the other creatures were (Genesis 2:20). Ellicott's is administrative: the law was deliberately left generic for those who had to apply it. Gill records how differently others treated the whole class — the Egyptian priests abstained from fish altogether, and Julian gave two reasons for it: that what is not sacrificed to the gods should not be eaten, and that creatures immersed in deep waters do not look up to heaven.

Henry reads the permission as generous rather than restrictive. The ancients accounted fish the most delicate of foods, and God laid little restraint on his people here — being a master who allows his servants not only for necessity but for delight. On the word abomination, repeated three times over, he is careful about its reach: it means count them unclean and keep at a distance, and it was an abomination only to Jews, the neighbouring nations lying under no such obligation. Wesley draws the same line from the words unto you — the creatures were not abominable in their own nature nor for other nations' food, so when the partition wall fell these distinctions were to cease. Henry turns the privilege into a burden willingly borne: Israel was honoured with peculiar privileges and therefore laid under peculiar restraints, and so God's spiritual Israel, dignified by the gospel covenant, must be mortified by its commands of self-denial.
13:
With the birds the method changes, and every witness marks the change. Gill notes that no sign is given at all, only names — twenty-four by Maimonides' count — so whoever knew the kinds might eat any other bird. Keil and Delitzsch count twenty varieties including the bat, almost all birds of prey or carrion; they pass on Knobel's judgement that the list is hardly meant to be exhaustive but names those which others ate, and against which Israel therefore needed a special prohibition. Ellicott finds the absence of criteria the more remarkable because after his kind keeps recurring, which shows kindred species were included and the definition left to those who administered the law. The rules they arrived at he gives in full: a bird is unclean if it snatches its food in the air and devours it without first dropping it, if it strikes with its talons and presses the prey down to tear pieces off with the beak, if it divides its feet on a branch two toes each side rather than three in front and one behind, or if its eggs are alike at both ends.

Clarke works instead from the roots of the names. The eagle is from a verb meaning to lacerate; the ossifrage is the bone-breaker; the osprey from a root meaning to be strong, which he takes for the black eagle Homer calls at once the swiftest and strongest of the feathered race. Ellicott identifies the second as the lammergeier, aptly called the vulture-eagle and standing in the list exactly between the two, which carries bones already stripped of flesh into the air and drops them on a chosen rock to get at the marrow. On the eagle he corrects a common claim: the assertion that the bird meant must be the Egyptian vulture, because the eagle disdains dead bodies and eats only what it kills, is erroneous — naturalists agree it will eat carrion while still fresh.

The identifications grow less certain as the list runs on. Ellicott would render the fourth name kite rather than vulture — the bird that sails on expanded wings and pauses as if suspended — and the fifth falcon rather than kite. On the raven all agree: Gill, Clarke, Ellicott, Keil and Delitzsch and Wesley all take the phrase to cover the whole genus, crows and rooks and jackdaws and jays together. Ellicott adds why the raven was chosen to feed the prophet — its greed and its unwillingness to part with anything even for its own young (1 Kings 17:4).

The hardest name is the one the English calls an owl. Gill, following the Septuagint, the Vulgate and both Targums, reads ostrich, and gives Pliny's account of a bird taller than a horseman and swifter than a horse; Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott agree. Clarke passes on Shaw's account of hearing them at night groan as if in the deepest agonies. The next name defeats everyone: Clarke reports Bochart's male ostrich and prefers Hasselquist's Oriental owl, while Ellicott, having weighed seven candidates, concludes that in such uncertainty it is best to leave the Authorised Version alone.

Two witnesses stand back and ask what the list is for. Henry sorts the forbidden birds four ways — birds of prey, since God would have his people abhor everything barbarous and not live by blood and rapine; solitary birds haunting dark and desolate places, since God's Israel should not be a melancholy people (Psalms 102:6; Isaiah 34:11); birds that feed on what is impure, as the stork on serpents; and birds the heathen used in divination. Wesley reaches nearly the same heads and adds an observation about the lost vocabulary: the true meaning of these words is now gone, and its going, not falling out without God's providence, may intimate the cessation of a law whose exact observance has since become impossible.
17:
The register runs on into names the translators plainly guessed at, and the witnesses say so. Gill notes that Ainsworth simply reverses the first and last of this group, taking the one for the great owl and the other for the little, and describes the great horned owl as a bird the size of a goose, with a head much of the figure of a cat's and clusters of black feathers rising over the ears. Clarke works the roots as before: the first name is the Hebrew word for a cup, which some think fits the pelican and its pouch; the second comes from a verb meaning to cast down, which the Septuagint rendered by the word for a cataract, and which he takes for the diver he has watched at sea drop like an arrow on a fish sighted from a great height; the third the Septuagint and Vulgate make the ibis.

Ellicott offers a textual observation here that is worth more than any single identification. Set these two verses beside the parallel list in Deuteronomy and the same six birds appear, but in a different order — the cormorant standing second here and sixth there. There can hardly be a doubt, he concludes, that the verse before us has been disturbed; and putting the cormorant sixth, as Deuteronomy has it, leaves the two kinds of owl standing naturally together, as they do in the other catalogue. He adds why two owls should be named separately rather than covered by after his kind: their habit of ejecting pellets, each containing sometimes four to seven skeletons of mice.

Of the next three, only one is what the English calls it. Nobody takes the first for a swan; Ellicott says flatly that whatever the word means it is certainly not that. The pelican both he and Clarke derive from a verb meaning to vomit up, from the pouch it empties against its breast to feed its young — and both trace the fable of a bird wounding itself to feed them with its blood to the red nail of the upper mandible touching the breast during the operation. Ellicott adds the picture behind a familiar psalm: the pelican retiring to a lonely place with its head leaning on its breast, almost motionless until hunger drives it back to the water (Psalms 102:6). The third he identifies as the Egyptian vulture, whose Hebrew name means the merciful, venerated there both as a scavenger and for its devotion to its young — so that the same word served for mother and for merciful.

The last three are named for their tempers. The stork's name means the kind or the pious, and Gill and Clarke and Ellicott all give the same reason: its care for its young and for its aged parents. Gill tells the story from Drusius of the fire at Delft, where the storks worked to save their young and, failing, threw themselves into the flames and perished with them. Why so admirable a bird should be unclean they answer the same way — it feeds on serpents, which Virgil and Juvenal both remark, and which is the reason the Mahometans give for the same prohibition. The heron's name, by contrast, means the angry, which Clarke thinks sufficiently descriptive of a bird that will attack a man at its nest — he knew a case of one nearly killed by a heron's bill near the eye. The list that began with the eagle ends with the bat, and Ellicott makes the arrangement deliberate: the vilest creature last, a thing between a bird and a mouse, placed there because it forms the connecting link between the winged bipeds and the quadrupeds that follow.
20:
A fourth class begins, and the phrase describing it needs care. Ellicott renders it all winged creeping things, and denies that upon all four is a count of feet at all: it describes walking with the body horizontal or near the ground, in contrast with the two-legged birds just dealt with, which is how the administrators of the law understood it. Clarke reaches the same conclusion from the impossibility of the literal reading — insects have six feet in general and many have far more, some being named centipedes and some millipedes. Gill lists what is actually meant: flies, fleas, bees, wasps, hornets, locusts. Wesley finds a moral in the very shape of such a creature, a flying thing that crawls and so degenerates from its proper nature, of a mongrel kind — which may intimate that apostates and mongrels in religion are abominable in the sight of God.

Ellicott follows the inclusion of the bee into a question it raises. If bees fall under this abomination, does their honey? Some concluded that it must, and that the honey so often named as the glory of the promised land was therefore grape-honey — the dibs still prepared in Syria — or the vegetable honey exuded by certain trees in the Sinai peninsula. The rule during the second Temple was indeed that whatever comes from unclean creatures is unclean, and the milk of unclean beasts and the eggs of unclean birds were forbidden accordingly. Yet bee-honey was expressly permitted, on the ground that it is not the direct produce of the insect but a preparation from the gathered juices of clean herbs; the Targum of Jonathan adds the exemption in so many words. John the Baptist, Ellicott concludes, acted in perfect obedience to the law when he ate the honey the bees had left in the crevices of the rocks (Matthew 3:4). The ban on honey in the meat-offerings is a separate matter, and turns on its tendency to ferment.

The exception carved out of the class is defined by a leg. Ellicott renders the clause which have knees above their hinder legs, meaning insects whose third pair is much longer and stronger, letting them raise themselves and leap a great distance; Clarke describes the same high-jointed hind legs projecting above the back. Keil and Delitzsch identify the creatures without hesitation as locusts, four varieties with their species, but admit the identification cannot be pressed, there being still a dearth of information on the natural history of the oriental locust. Ellicott gives the canonical marks of a clean locust — four front feet, four wings, two springing feet, and wings long and broad enough to cover most of the body.

On the four names the witnesses do agree about one thing. Clarke insists the third cannot be the beetle, since no beetle was ever eaten by man in any country of the universe; the Hebrew, from roots meaning to shake and the foot, describes something nimble, exactly as the English grasshopper and the French sauterelle do. Ellicott makes all four locusts on the plain ground that the context enumerates four kinds of one insect, and reports what the second-Temple authorities said of each — that this one has a hump and a tail, that one a tail and no hump. That they were genuinely eaten nobody doubts. Henry notes that several sorts were very good meat and much used, and that John the Baptist lived on them in the desert; Wesley lists the Ethiopians, Libyans and Parthians as eating them and supposes the eastern kinds larger and better nourishment than ours; Clarke ate them himself at second hand, reporting that Shaw had them in Barbary fried and salted and found they tasted very like crayfish, and that whole tribes lived so freely on them that the Greeks called them locust-eaters.
24:
The subject changes from the table to the touch, and the rule is graded. Keil and Delitzsch set it out: whoever touched a carcase was unclean until the evening and then washed himself; whoever carried one was more deeply affected, and had to wash his clothes as well. Ellicott gives the same distinction as a principle — pollution by carrying is greater than pollution by touching — and adds what the second-Temple administrators made of the shorter formula: wherever the law says a man shall wash his clothes it includes bathing the body, omitted here only for brevity, and the Samaritan text and some Hebrew manuscripts actually carry the fuller phrase. He hears an allusion to it in those who came out of the great tribulation and washed their robes (Revelation 7:14). Wesley states the practical effect in a line: such a man was shut out both from the court of God's house and from free conversation with other men.

What until the even covers is defined by the Hebrew day. Ellicott explains that contact defiled for the rest of the day and until a new one began at sunset, and during those hours the man could not enter the sanctuary, touch anything sacred, or mix with the clean, since his defilement passed to whatever he touched. Henry finds a purpose in the time limit that nobody else reaches for: the uncleanness continued only till evening to signify that all ceremonial pollutions were to come to an end by the death of Christ in the evening of the world. He turns it to daily use as well — that we should learn, by renewing our repentance every night for the sins of the day, to cleanse ourselves from what we have contracted, and not lie down in our uncleanness.

Henry also guards the rule from being read as a moral one. These carcases were not defiling to the conscience, and it was no sin against God to touch them unless it were done in contempt of the law; in many cases somebody must of necessity touch them in order to remove them. What was contracted was a ceremonial uncleanness, which for a time barred a man from the tabernacle and the holy things. And he notes the limit on the other side, which is what makes the whole system workable: the living animals might be touched freely, horses and dogs among them, because Israel was allowed to use them for service — it is only the dead body that defiles, and what may not be eaten must not be handled dead.

That distinction, obvious as it looks, was the point of a famous quarrel, and Ellicott reports it. The Pharisees read the pronoun in the twenty-sixth verse as referring to the carcases, so that only a dead unclean animal defiled; on that reading camels and asses and horses could be used in daily life, as the rest of scripture plainly shows they were. The Sadducees took the same pronoun of the living animals, and held that touching any beast named in this list defiled at all. The difference this made to domestic life and social intercourse, Ellicott says, can hardly be described — for on the Sadducees' doctrine it was exceedingly difficult to remain undefiled as soon as a man stepped outside his own door. Clarke and Gill fill in the last category named, the beasts that go on their paws: creatures whose feet are not divided in two but end in something like a hand, the lion and the bear, the ape and the monkey, the wolf, the dog and the cat.
29:
Eight small creatures are named, and hardly one of them is securely identified. Keil and Delitzsch say so at the outset: the early translators tell us nothing certain about several of these names, and it is still undecided how they should be rendered — the third has been made a shrew-mouse by the Septuagint, a groaning lizard by Bochart, a gecko by Rosenmüller, the whole family of monitors by Leyrer, and by Knobel the great river lizard of the Nile. Against that last they raise an objection that settles it: Moses can hardly have supposed an animal four feet long, resembling a crocodile, might drop dead into a pot or a dish.

Where the witnesses can be definite they are, and Ellicott is definite by way of the men who had to administer the law. On the first name he sets out their description — a creature lodging in the holes of walls and in ditches, inordinately voracious, killing prey much larger than itself and carrying it off in its mouth, especially destructive to poultry, piercing the skulls of hens with pointed teeth, lapping water from a vessel and hiding bright objects in holes — and concludes that this can only be the weasel, not the mole, whatever the Arabic cognate suggests. Clarke, following Bochart, prefers the mole for exactly that reason, its burrowing under the surface answering the root. On the second all agree it is a mouse; Ellicott adds that its voracity made it the scourge of the field, that killing them was permitted even on the middle days of the great festivals, and that Jews still brand a malicious person a wicked mouse.

On the third Ellicott makes an argument that is worth the space. It is certainly not the tortoise, since Maimonides expressly says the serpent, the frog and the tortoise are not defiling at all; and the second-Temple authorities plainly meant the toad, as appears from their discussion of a man who has touched a creature and cannot decide whether it was a frog, which does not defile, or this, which does. It is the toad and not the tortoise that can be mistaken for a frog, and the Hebrew name — the swollen one — fits its thick squat body exactly.

The rest divide the commentators. Clarke reads lizard after lizard, taking one for the mongoose that Indian households keep to clear the place of snakes; Ellicott makes the same name a chameleon and passes on the Talmud's story of Shem in the ark, who could not discover what the creature fed on until he broke a pomegranate and a worm fell out, which it devoured at once. On the last two they converge — a snail, whose constant slime was thought to dissolve it as it went, and which the psalm accordingly calls the thing that melteth (Psalms 58:8); and a mole, eyeless, burrowing, destroying the roots.

Why these eight and no others is the question the last verse of the group raises, and two answers are given. Ellicott renders the phrase these shall be the most unclean, taking them to be pre-eminently so among all the creeping things. Keil and Delitzsch deny that: the words mean neither that these were the only unclean swarmers nor that they carried a greater uncleanness, since every unclean animal defiled the person and even the clothes of anyone who carried it. What is peculiar to these eight is where they live. They were commonly found in houses, so there was far more fear of their falling dead upon objects in daily use — which is why the instructions that follow are about pots and clothes rather than about persons. Gill adds the rule the later doctors built on the same verse, that with such a creature the blood defiles as the flesh does.
32:
What follows is a graded law of contagion running through a household's furniture. Keil and Delitzsch give the two branches: anything of wood or cloth or leather on which such a creature fell was to be put into water and was unclean until evening, after which it was clean again; but an earthen vessel into whose interior one fell was unclean together with all its contents, and had to be broken — because the uncleanness was absorbed into the clay and could not be got out again by washing. Ellicott gives the same reason and adds that the contents were polluted with it.

The categories are then defined narrowly, and Ellicott reports the definitions from the second Temple. A vessel of wood means anything grown out of the earth — bulrushes, reeds, wicker, nutshells, bark. Raiment means woven stuff of something that grows on dry land, so that cloth made from a sea-grown material contracted nothing. Skin means the hide of land animals only, aquatic skins being exempt. And sack, as the parallel in Numbers shows, means the coarse stuff of goats' hair, as distinct from the finer weave the other word covers. Clarke furnishes the same list from an Arab tent — the wooden bowls, the trunks and baskets covered with skin, the goat-skins used for churning milk, the hair-cloth for carrying goods from place to place.

Ellicott adds a limit that made the law livable, and a second quarrel about it. Only a portion of a carcase with flesh still on it defiled; skins, hair, bones, horns, hoofs and sinews were exempt, and were accordingly worked up into domestic implements. The Sadducees would not have it, holding every portion of every unclean animal defiling whatever its state, and forbidding its use in any vessel at all — the same division of judgement that ran through the question of touching a living beast.

Two clauses about food draw the closest reading. Keil and Delitzsch reject the traditional rendering of the meat clause — that the food is defiled by water coming out of such a vessel — on the plain ground that the Hebrew word, without an article, cannot mean such water; what is meant is food prepared with water, which becomes unclean if the creature falls dead on it. Ellicott records the rule that grew from it: food becomes liable only when some liquid has been poured on it, and stays liable afterwards even if it has dried again, while food never moistened does not become defiled at all — the liquids in question being seven, water and dew and oil and wine and milk and blood and honey. Wesley reaches the same distinction by common sense: what is dressed in water in a polluted vessel is unclean, but not what is eaten dry, like bread or fruit, because the water sooner receives the pollution into itself and carries it to the food.

The last clause reaches the fixtures, and Clarke supplies the picture. The ranges for pots are not furniture but a hole dug in the floor of the tent about a foot and a half deep, three-quarters of it laid about with stones and the fourth left open for throwing in fuel; Ellicott describes the oven as a baking-pot wide at the bottom and narrow at the top, so shaped to hold the heat. Both were earthenware, and both, on the same principle as the vessel, had to be broken down.
36:
Three exemptions follow, and every witness notices that they are exemptions of mercy. A spring or a cistern is not defiled, and Keil and Delitzsch give the reason in a phrase — the uncleanness would be carried off at once by the fresh supply. Clarke says the same of running water, or of reservoirs large enough that the water soon purifies itself. Ellicott makes the exemption depend on the constant change of water in such a receptacle, notes that the second-Temple rule confined it to collections of water actually in the ground and not to water standing in vessels, and then states plainly what the provision means: when it is borne in mind how few wells and cisterns there are in the East, and how scarce water is, the mercy of this law will be apparent.

Wesley presses that further than anyone. Of this exemption, he says, no reason can be given but the will of the lawgiver and his merciful condescension to men's necessities, water being scarce in those countries — and for the same reason God would have the ceremonial law of sacrifices give place to the law of mercy. It is a striking thing to find that principle drawn out of a rule about a dead mouse in a well; but the rule is doing exactly what Wesley says, setting a man's need for water above a ceremonial defilement.

The exemption is not unlimited, and Ellicott marks the line. The water is spared, but the man who reaches into it to lift the carcase out is not: the carcase remains a source of defilement wherever it lies, so whoever handles it to remove it is unclean, exactly as he would have been anywhere else.

Seed for sowing is spared on the same principle, and Ellicott makes the parallel explicit. What underlies the immunity of living water underlies the immunity of a living plant: grain destined for the ground is not defiled by a carcase found among it, because the growing plant draws new elements from below and fresh moisture from above, undergoing as many changes on its way as spring water does. The rule that came of it he gives in two lines — whatever is fixed in the ground does not contract defilement, and plants are not defiled until they are gathered. Keil and Delitzsch put it more physically: the uncleanness attaching to dry seed externally would simply be absorbed by the earth.

Wet seed is the exception to the exception, and here the reasoning of all three converges. Once the grain has been softened by water the defilement can penetrate the substance of the seed, so that it would carry uncleanness into the fruit; Ellicott compares it to a porous clay vessel saturated beyond cleansing. Wesley adds the argument from necessity that the rest of the section runs on — dry seed was spared because it was necessary provision for a man and because the earth would work its alterations on it, whereas wet seed was not fit to be sown at once, so the necessity that excused the one cannot be pleaded for the other.
39:
The chapter turns last to the clean animal that was never killed. Ellicott defines the case exactly: a beast that is both cloven-footed and ruminant, and so lawful food, but which has not been properly slaughtered, having died of disease or accident. Wesley adds the other way it happens, that it was killed by a wild beast, and puts his finger on what is common to both — in neither case was the blood poured forth, as it is when a beast is killed by men for food or for sacrifice. Gill lists the animals concerned, the ox and the sheep and the goat and the deer, and makes the same point: what would have been very lawful to eat is not lawful now.

What such a carcase does is what an unclean carcase does. Ellicott says the body is to be regarded exactly as the dead body of an unclean animal, and defiles by contact; Keil and Delitzsch set the rule alongside the earlier one and note that the grading is identical — touching defiles till evening, carrying defiles and requires the clothes to be washed as well. Ellicott adds that this was restricted during the second Temple to quadrupeds, wild or domestic, and not applied to birds or fishes.

The limit is the same one that has run through the section, and it is what allowed ordinary trades to continue. Only the flesh defiles. Skin, bones, sinews, horns and claws are clean — so much so, Ellicott notes, that the sacred scriptures themselves were written on prepared skins, and the horns of the sanctuary's trumpets came from the same source. That was the ruling of the Pharisees; the Samaritans and Sadducees held such parts polluting, which would have made both the scrolls and the trumpets impossible.

On the eating, one word is doing a great deal of work, and two witnesses supply it. Ellicott says the clause contemplates a man who ate ignorantly, since for wilful transgression the penalty was not a washing but excision from the people. Wesley says the same in his own terms: unwittingly, for if a man did it knowingly it was a presumptuous sin against an express law and was punished by cutting off. The distinction matters for reading the whole chapter. Everything from the touching of a carcase to the breaking of an oven belongs to a system of ceremonial defilement with a remedy attached — water, a broken pot, the coming of evening. Deliberate contempt of the law is a different matter altogether, and is dealt with elsewhere and far more severely.
41:
The creeping things are now forbidden as food, which had not been said before. Gill notices the gap and why it is filled here: the earlier passage made these eight defile by their carcases, but never expressly said they were not to be eaten. He also gives the working definition — nothing is called a creeping thing but what is low, with short feet, and is not seen unless it moves — and takes the qualifier upon the earth to be doing real work. Ellicott spells out what it excludes. Worms bred inside food do not creep upon the earth, so the maggots in figs and dates and berries, the mites in peas and beans and lentils, the grubs in cheese and the insects under the skin of a fish were all held permitted; only when such a creature leaves the thing it was bred in and crawls on the ground does it fall under the ban.

Three classes are then named, and Ellicott sorts them. Those that move on the under part of the body, serpents and serpentine worms; those with four legs that move like reptiles, scorpions and beetles; and those whose feet are so short and so many that they cannot easily be seen, caterpillars and centipedes and millipedes — for which the last phrase is better rendered whatsoever hath many feet. Wesley matches the classes to plainer creatures: worms and snakes for the first, toads and divers serpents for the second. Gill passes on the older reading of the opening clause, that going upon the belly is the curse pronounced on the serpent — and then, characteristically, records that serpents have all the same been eaten and reckoned delicious, by a people the Greeks called serpent-eaters and by the Troglodytes of Pliny.

Clarke and Keil and Delitzsch both pause over a scribal curiosity in the middle of it. One letter in the word for belly is written larger than the rest, and a Masoretic note explains why: it is the middle letter of the law, which makes this the middle verse of the Pentateuch. It is a small thing, but it tells you what kind of book the scribes thought they were copying — one counted letter by letter.

Calvin uses the summing-up to state the chapter's point as he understands it, and it is the same position he has taken throughout. God does not here invite them to take care of their health, nor warn them of disease; he bids them beware of defiling themselves, and the clearer explanation follows at once in the words for I am the LORD your God. Lest they should suppose the main part of religion lay in external ceremonies, they were to consider the nature of God himself: being a Spirit, he would be worshipped only spiritually, so that holiness is connected with the distinction of meats only instrumentally — their abstinence had no other object than that they should consecrate themselves to him.

From that Calvin turns on the failure, and the image he chooses is the sharpest thing in the chapter. The superstition of the Jews was inexcusable when they contented themselves with trifling observances — as if a man should learn the letters of the alphabet and never afterwards care to join them into words and read. Nor did they stop there: men lay hold of anything that will sustain them in hypocrisy, and they heaped up rites nobody had asked for, water of lustration always in use even when they knew of no defilement, and an anxious labour in the washing of cups and platters. Ellicott makes the same point from the wording, that a man who eats what is abominable renders himself abominable — the phrase in the parallel place being rendered not yourselves but your souls.
44:
The reason for the whole chapter is given last, and it is not a reason from hygiene or from natural history. Ellicott states it plainly: the Lord who is their God is himself holy, and a people who are to have communion with him must be holy too — which is why the apostle takes up these very words and applies them to Christians, that as he who called you is holy, so be ye holy in all manner of conversation (1 Peter 1:15-16). Henry marks the same quotation and its force: a precept that stands here in the middle of abrogated laws is stamped in the epistle as a gospel precept.

Henry's exposition of what the law was for is the fullest in the chapter, and he begins by ruling out the two readings most likely to occur to a modern reader. It was not intended merely for a bill of fare, nor as a physician's directions about diet. It was meant to teach three things: to put a difference between good and evil, since it could not be all one what they did when it was not all one what they ate; to keep a constant observance of God's law even in the commonest actions, so that eating and drinking are done by rule and to the glory of God (1 Corinthians 10:31); and to distinguish them from every neighbouring people as a nation set apart. On the warning against self-defilement he is briefer and harder: by having fellowship with sin, which is abominable, we make ourselves abominable — and that man is truly miserable who is abominable in the sight of God, as none are but those who make themselves so.

Wesley draws the same conclusion and makes the negative explicit. All these cautions about eating and touching, he says, were not for any real uncleanness in the creatures at all, but so that by diligent observation of such rules the people might learn to avoid moral pollution with greater care.

Clarke dissents, and the disagreement has been running under the whole chapter. He denies that God forbade these foods merely as a sovereign: he forbade them because he knew they would injure body and mind alike, the connection between the two being real however little we comprehend it. Ruminating animals concoct their food better and yield more nutritious flesh; the solid-footed and the many-toed afford a gross nutriment; scaleless fish abound in fat that few stomachs can digest. In all this, he says, God shows himself the tender father of a numerous family, pointing out to inexperienced children the aliments that will hurt them. Yet Clarke ends where Henry and Wesley and Calvin end. The grand design of the whole was that they should be holy and resemble a holy God; and no faith in any creed, no religious observance, no acts of benevolence, no mortification or contrition can be a substitute for that — we must be made partakers of the divine nature.

Clarke adds one argument nobody else offers, drawn from the state of the text itself. Since no Jew now living can say with certainty what most of these animals were, a man observing the law today might break it repeatedly without knowing. From the difficulty of the vocabulary he concludes that the law itself must be considered abrogated. The last reason the chapter gives is the one every witness treats as decisive: I am the LORD that bringeth you up out of the land of Egypt. Henry puts it as an argument from gratitude — that a people so lately dignified with distinguishing favours might cheerfully submit to distinguishing laws — and Ellicott notes how often the rest of scripture appeals to that same deliverance, both to bind obedience and to expose ingratitude.
46:
The chapter closes with its own table of contents, and Ellicott notices that the table is not in the order of the chapter. The law itself took the four classes as land animals, water animals, birds and swarming things; the summary lists them as land animals, birds, water animals and swarming things. He observes that exactly the same shift occurs in the summary that closes the sacrificial law — which suggests the re-ordering is a habit of these colophons rather than a slip.

The last verse states the purpose, and Ellicott would render it that ye may put difference, the same phrase used of the priests' charge in the preceding chapter. The design, in other words, is not to publish a list but to train a faculty: to give the administrators of the law and the people alike the marks by which they can tell for themselves what is clean from what is not. Gill's summary of the chapter comes to the same thing — that by such descriptions and distinctions the Israelites would be able to make the difference and know what was to be eaten.

One oddity in the wording drew a further ruling. The same word for beast stands in both halves of the last clause, without the qualifiers clean and unclean, and the second-Temple authorities concluded from that that a single clean animal is in view under two different conditions: edible when sound, and not edible when it has organic defects or disease. The canon they framed for soundness was reproductive — an animal is perfectly sound when it is capable of conceiving and bringing forth young — and Ellicott notes that the Septuagint's odd rendering of the word here by viviparous points the same way.

What became of the law is the note both Henry and Wesley end on. It was a statute for ever, they agree, in the sense that it lasted as long as that economy did; and it was expressly repealed by the voice from heaven to Peter, having already been virtually set aside by the death of Christ (Acts 10:15). Meat does not commend us to God, nothing is unclean of itself, and what defiles a man is not what goes into his mouth but what comes out of his heart.

Henry will not let the liberty stand without a discipline beside it, and his three applications close the chapter better than a summary would. Give thanks that we are not under this yoke, every creature of God being now allowed as good and nothing to be refused. Stand fast in the liberty Christ has given, and beware the doctrines that command abstinence from meats and would revive Moses again. And then the third, which cuts the other way: be strictly and conscientiously temperate in the use of what God has allowed — for if God's law has given us liberty, let us lay restraints upon ourselves, and never feed ourselves without fear, lest our table become a snare. Set a knife to thy throat, he says, if thou be a man given to appetite (Proverbs 23:2); nature is content with little, grace with less, but lust with nothing.
